summary: Describes a key exchange method for SSH in which the server proposes new groups for the Diffie-Hellman exchange to the client. The groups need not be fixed and can change over time. It is standards-track.

plainLanguage.summary: Two people make a shared secret by mixing numbers. Here the server picks which numbers to mix, and can change them over time.

questions: what is ssh diffie-hellman group exchange
what is a safe prime in ssh
why does ssh use group exchange
subtitle: Lets an SSH server pick fresh Diffie-Hellman groups on demand instead of everyone using one fixed group.

tldr.problem: SSH key exchange used the single fixed group of diffie-hellman-group1-sha1, which the authors feared could be attacked with heavy precomputation or better discrete logarithm algorithms over the years.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends a minimum, preferred and maximum group size; the server answers with a safe prime p and a generator g that fit, and the usual Diffie-Hellman exchange runs over that group.
tldr.outcome: Two new methods, diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1 and diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256, let servers rotate groups so attackers have less reason to precompute for any one of them. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 8270.

today: RFC 4419 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 8270; it has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Fixed Groups Are a Worry
sections.content:
SSH protects remote logins, and its initial key exchange used the diffie-hellman-group1-sha1 method, which prescribes one fixed group for all operations. The Diffie-Hellman exchange gives both sides a shared secret that neither could determine alone, and in SSH the exchange is signed with the server's host key to authenticate the host.

Its strength rests on the difficulty of the Discrete Logarithm Problem. Because SSH is expected to be used for many years, the authors feared that extensive precomputation and more efficient algorithms against a fixed group could become a threat.

Letting the server propose new groups reduces the incentive to precompute. The server can compute new groups continuously in the background.
sections.plainLanguage: If everyone plays the same board game with the same board, a cheater can study that board for years. If the host keeps swapping the board, studying one of them is not worth the trouble.

sections.title: Safe Primes and Generators
sections.content:
The server keeps a list of safe primes and matching generators. A prime p is safe if p = 2q + 1 and q is also prime. New primes can be generated in the background.

The generator g should be chosen so that the order of the generated subgroup does not factor into small primes: with p = 2q + 1, the order has to be either q or p - 1. If it is p - 1, the generator is a primitive root, and the exponents reach all possible public values evenly instead of cycling through a smaller subset.

Servers and clients SHOULD support moduli of k bits where 1024 <= k <= 8192. The recommended values for min and max are 1024 and 8192. The server should return the smallest group it knows that is larger than the requested size; if none is larger, it SHOULD return the largest it knows. The returned group SHOULD be at least 1024 bits.
sections.plainLanguage: Not every number makes a good game board. The server only uses specially shaped big numbers that are known to behave well, and it picks the one closest to the size the client asked for.

sections.title: The Exchange Step by Step
sections.content:
The client (C) and server (S) have already exchanged their KEXINIT messages. Then:

  • C sends min || n || max: the smallest acceptable group size, the preferred size and the largest acceptable size, in bits.
  • S finds the group that best matches and sends p || g.
  • C picks a random x with 1 < x < (p-1)/2, computes e = g^x mod p and sends e.
  • S picks a random y with 0 < y < (p-1)/2, computes f = g^y mod p and the shared secret K = e^y mod p. It computes the exchange hash H, signs it with its private host key, and sends K_S || f || s.
  • C checks that K_S really is the server's host key, computes K = f^x mod p and the same H, and verifies the signature.

A client may accept the host key without verifying it, but the RFC says doing so makes the protocol insecure against active attacks.

Both sides MUST NOT send or accept e or f values outside the range [1, p-1], and MUST accept K only if 1 < K < p - 1, to prevent confinement attacks.
sections.plainLanguage: The client says what size of board it likes, the server hands over a board, each side secretly mixes in a private number, and they swap the mixed results. Both can then work out the same shared secret, and the server signs to prove it is the real server.

sections.title: Messages and the Exchange Hash
sections.content:
Four messages carry the exchange. SSH_MSG_KEY_DH_GEX_REQUEST holds three uint32 values: min, n and max. SSH_MSG_KEX_DH_GEX_GROUP holds p and g as mpints. SSH_MSG_KEX_DH_GEX_INIT holds e. SSH_MSG_KEX_DH_GEX_REPLY holds the host key and certificates, f, and the signature of H.

The exchange hash H covers the client and server version strings, both KEXINIT payloads, the host key, min, n, max, p, g, e, f and K. It authenticates the exchange as set out in RFC 4253.

Section 5 lists the message numbers. They live in a name space private to this document, not assigned by IANA. SSH_MSG_KEX_DH_GEX_REQUEST_OLD (30) exists for backward compatibility: the client sends only n, and the hash uses only n in place of min || n || max.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages are like four notes passed back and forth. The last one carries a stamp that is made from everything said so far, so any tampering would show.

sections.title: The Two Key Exchange Methods
sections.content:
The RFC defines two method names. diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha1 uses SHA-1 as the hash, and diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256 uses SHA-256. The hash is called HASH in the exchange, and the public key algorithm used for the signature is negotiated through the KEXINIT messages.

For the SHA-256 method, the same hash must also be used in the key derivation pseudo-random function, as required by the "Output from Key Exchange" section of RFC 4253.
sections.plainLanguage: There are two flavors of the same recipe, each using a different kind of scrambler. Both sides must agree which flavor they are using.

sections.title: Implementation Advice
sections.content:
One technique is to pick the generator first and then sieve only for primes that work with it: 2 when p (mod 24) = 11, and 5 when p (mod 10) = 3 or 7. Using 2 is recommended because it improves multiplication performance. It is usable even when it is not a primitive root, since it still covers half of the possible residues.

To speed up the exchange, either side may shorten its private exponent, which should be at least twice as long as the key material generated from the shared secret. Appendix A gives a method for generating a k-bit safe prime for which 2 is a generator, adapted from the Handbook of Applied Cryptography.
sections.plainLanguage: Picking the simplest possible starting number makes the math quicker for the computer, as long as the other rules are still met.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The protocol aims to be simple and uses only well-understood primitives. Using many moduli stops an attacker from precalculating exchange values and discourages spending resources on analysing any particular modulus.

Only safe primes should be used. With a random prime modulus, short private exponents make the discrete logarithm easy, but the cited authors state that this does not apply to safe primes. The least significant bit of the private exponent can be recovered when the modulus is a safe prime, which is not a problem if the exponent is big enough. The security considerations of RFC 4251 also apply.
sections.plainLanguage: Changing the board often makes cheating harder, and using only well-behaved boards avoids known tricks. The private numbers just need to be big enough.
